[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p514#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عصفور | reports | Ibn ʿAṣfūr says using the singular al-najm for stars is forced by poetic necessity and cites a verse about the star’s disappearance.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p514#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The sukūn in the reading is explained either as a lightened pronunciation or as a dialect form.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p514#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | An unusual explanation calls the landmarks long, thin, snake-like fish in the Indian Ocean; their appearance signals arrival in India and safety on the route from Yemen.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p514#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | Most readers have al-najm as a generic collective noun; Ibn Waththāb and al-Ḥasan read it with dammah, and authorities transmit these forms from ʿĀṣim’s circle.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the star supplies the direction for the qibla and guides travelers on land and sea.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | An unnamed view identifies the star as the pole star, which does not move.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another view identifies the star as the Pleiades.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | An anonymous poem describes the rising star helping travelers find crossings of the Euphrates.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p515/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A second poem links the rising Pleiades with grass being bent and harvested.

[SAMIN-DURR:16:16/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | He compares the dropped long vowel in this form with خيام shortened to خيم.
[SAMIN-DURR:16:16/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عصفور | reports | He calls النجم a poetic necessity for النجوم and cites a line where the word means the stars.

[BURHAN:v2p12/r8] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | One cannot claim divine favor for something forbidden; the author rejects the view that the favor is creation of an ability to endure it.

[BURSEVI:v5p16/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | At night in deserts and seas, travelers navigate by stars where no other landmark is available.

[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Signs are landmarks travelers use, such as mountains, water sources, and even the smell of soil, which can show whether a route is frequented; masafa is connected to smelling.

[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عيسى | reports | Ibn Isa interprets signs broadly as anything that conveys what is intended, including writing, words, gestures, or appearance.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The author favors the initial interpretation as landmarks and calls the most unusual alternative a far-fetched report of long, thin, snake-like fish in the Indian Sea whose appearance signals reaching India and safety.

[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#3/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | If the pronoun singles out Quraysh, their special familiarity with star navigation makes considering the sign and thanking God through tawhid especially binding on them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#3/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some take the verse as a basis for learning stars to determine times, the qibla, and routes; learning what enables these is permissible.
[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#3/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو العباس أحمد بن البناء | reports | Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn al-Banna says exact qibla determination from stars is difficult or impossible: a star's position over Mecca does not transfer to another city, and al-Jady's shoulder or side position works only on a particular, uncertain meridian.

[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi restricts the star to the Pleiades, the two Farqads, Banat Naʿsh, and al-Jady.

[ALUSI-FULL:v14p116#3/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحسن وابن وثاب | reports | Al-Hasan reads the word with two dammas and Ibn Waththab with damma then sukun; both are plural forms, like سقف and رهن, and the sukun is either for ease or dialect.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p120#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The passage shifts to evidence and gratitude for great creatures on Earth’s surface that benefit people; calling their creation ‘casting’ pictures them as additions placed on a completed Earth, perhaps created later.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p120#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | He also proposes that mountains formed from debris cast off by celestial bodies and rain formed rivers; ‘casting’ fits these naturally and extends to routes and markers by generalization, as in 54:25 for giving revelation. | mentions 54:25
